KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 2:35 AM EDT...Current sfc analysis shows 
a 1032 mb sfc high centered just east of Cape Cod, with the 
remnant circulation of Isaias tracking over Tennessee. Deep 
southerly flow ahead of this sfc low has allowed widespread 
cirrus to overspread the region, with increasing coverage and 
thickening of the high clouds expected as we head through the 
rest of the night. Given our proximity to the sfc high, winds 
are calm across the region, so areas north and east of the 
Capital District we able to radiate into the mid 30s where the 
clouds were thinner early tonight. However, with thickening 
clouds moving into the region, temperatures likely hold steady 
or even rise slightly as we head towards sunrise. 

Today into tonight, the remnant, weakened sfc low of Isaias tracks 
south of Long Island. As it approaches, moisture begins to 
increase (PWATs getting up to 1.5", highest in southern areas). 
The best low to mid-level forcing (warm advection) remains near 
the southern edge of our CWA near I-84, but guidance still 
suggests there will be a band of mid-level FGEN further north 
near I-90, and the right entrance region of an anticyclonically
curved upper jet streak to our north will help the precip 
shield expand across our area today. Based on current radar and 
CAMs, rain begins in the southeastern Catskills shortly after 
sunrise, slowly overspreading the rest of the region through the
day. It may take until late afternoon/evening until the rain 
makes its way into the eastern ADKs, upper Hudson Valley, and 
southern VT. Rain becomes steady shortly after it begins, 
falling light to occasionally moderate at times. Given lack of 
any real instability, rainfall rates look to remain under a 
quarter to half inch per hour. Total rainfall amounts generally 
look to average a half inch to an inch, but our far northern 
areas may see a little less, with some localized 1-1.5" amounts 
possible near I-84 and in the eastern Catskills due to some SE 
upslope enhancement. Given that the southern half of our area 
hasn't seen appreciable rain in over 10 days this will be a very
beneficial rainfall. Rainfall amounts and rates look too low to
cause any flooding concerns. Today will be fairly cool (highs 
in the 50s to around 60) due to the widespread clouds and rain.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Rain tapers to showers overnight tonight, coming to 
an end by early tomorrow morning. Tomorrow looks like a tranquil 
weather day with a narrow ridge of high pressure at the sfc building 
over the region. Rising heights and a slightly warmer airmass aloft 
will allow highs to climb into the mid 60s to low 70s, which is
a few degrees above normal for this time of year.

Monday night into Tuesday, a sfc low tracking into the Great Lakes 
region will help lift a warm front across our region. This sfc low 
will track to the north of our are Tuesday into early 
Wednesday, dragging a cold front across the region. Guidance 
has trended further north and slower with this system since 
yesterday, with the cold front now not expected to arrive until 
Tuesday night or even early Wednesday. Therefore, PoPs have 
decreased for areas of I-90 on Tuesday. Temperatures south of 
I-90 may also need to be increased from the current forecast for
Tuesday afternoon if this forecast trend continues, as mid 70s 
are not off the table there. Further north trend with the track 
of the sfc low would also put more of our region into the warm 
sector. With Showalter values <0 Tuesday afternoon/evening, have
expanded the slight chance for thunder to cover much of our 
area. Despite impressive low-level shear profiles, the 
combination of instability remaining mainly elevated and 
overnight timing of the frontal passage should prevent any 
severe weather.

Wednesday, cooler air infiltrates the region behind the cold
front. Temperatures are expected to run a few degrees below 
normal, especially by Thursday and Friday. Wednesday and 
possibly Thursday look breezy ahead of sfc high pressure that 
will build overhead for the end of the workweek. By the end of 
the week or early next weekend, guidance continues to suggest 
that a fairly strong sfc low will track somewhere near (likely 
west) of our region. This would bring additional chances for 
showers, and perhaps a brief warmup depending on the strength of
the storm and its exact track. Another, more impressive cold 
shot appears likely behind this system next Saturday or Sunday.
